transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-12-03
Start: 15:30 PT
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Avery Cole (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Maya Lin (Redwood DevAdv), Dr. Lena Morales (CTO, NovaHealth), Marco Ruiz (Platform Eng), Priya Khanna (Data PM)

Summary: Quick demo of Redwood Console + API focused on JSON mode / schema contracts and safe tool calling. Showed two flows: 1) strict JSON mode for structured clinical summarization with schema validation and canonicalization; 2) tool/function calling demo where the model returns a JSON payload that triggers a safe webhook/db write via a secured connector. Discussed security, SSO, and pilot next steps.

Topics: JSON schema enforcement, Console UI for contracts, API params (json_schema, strict_mode), guardrails and canonicalizers, function/tool calling, webhooks, cost/latency tradeoffs, SOC2/KMS.

[00:00] Avery: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intros, then Samir will jump into a short Console demo around JSON contracts and how we do safe tool calls.
[00:22] Lena: Hi, thanks. We're mainly curious about locking outputs to a schema — we have to feed downstream analytics and EHR ingestion, so the fewer manual fixes the better.
[00:35] Samir: Totally. We'll show the JSON mode — in Console it's a checkbox + schema editor, and via API you can pass a json_schema object and set strict_mode=true. When strict_mode is on the runtime will validate the model output and attempt canonicalization or rerun with a focused prompt.
[00:58] Marco: How deterministic is that? If the model misses a field do you reject or patch?
[01:05] Samir: Good question. There are three behaviours: reject (fast fail), patch with a canonicalizer (we map close tokens to expected enum values), or re-ask the model with a targeted clarification. You can configure per-route.
[01:25] Priya: And how do you define the schema? JSON-schema?
[01:30] Samir: Yes, it's close to JSON Schema Draft 7 with a few Redwood extensions — e.g., "enum_synonyms" to map likely variants, and a "safety_constraints" block for allowed value sets. We'll show an example for clinical severity and coded diagnosis.
[01:45] Maya: I'll share my screen.
[01:47] [screen share starts]
[01:52] Maya: This is the Console route editor. Here I've got the route "clin-summarize/v1" — note the toggle "JSON Mode". If I open the schema editor you can see the schema with required fields: patient_id, encounter_date ISO8601, diagnosis_code (ICD10), severity enum. See the enum_synonyms mapping for 'mild' -> ['mild', 'low', '1'].
[02:23] Lena: Nice. What about partial text outputs? Our notes are messy, often shorthand.
[02:29] Samir: That's where the canonicalizer helps — we apply normalization helpers (date parsers, unit normalizers). Also you can set confidence thresholds; if the model returns low confidence or ambiguous tokens we'll either re-ask or flag for human review.
[02:48] Marco: Can development teams run this locally? We have a private deployment need.
[02:54] Avery: Yes — the same Console + route configs translate to Redwood Private or Dedicated. The control plane syncs configs; their private runtime enforces the same schema and routing rules.
[03:10] Priya: Give us a quick API example.
[03:14] Samir: Sure. The API call looks like: POST /v1/generate with body {"model":"redwood-structured-1","prompt":"...","json_schema": <schema>,"strict_mode":true,"on_failure":"rerun"}. The response will either be {"status":"ok","output_json":{...}} or {"status":"validation_error","errors":[...]} if reject. We also support streaming partial JSON tokens so you can show progress in the UI.
[03:50] Marco: Latency impact?
[03:53] Samir: There's a small added CPU/latency for validation and canonicalization, typically +30–120ms depending on schema complexity. The bigger hit is when you re-ask the model which is another generation call — that multiplies token costs. In Optimize we can suggest softer strategies like prefix caching and targeted re-asks to keep costs down.
[04:20] Lena: Can we attach tool calls — for instance, when a summary contains an action like 'order follow-up lab' we want the model to call our internal workflow API, but only after an explicit human approval.
[04:34] Samir: Yep. Two patterns: synchronous tool call with pre-conditions (model returns a structured action blob but route enforces an approval flag), or asynchronous webhook where the validated JSON is posted to a secure connector that requires a signed webhook signature and RBAC.
[04:50] Maya: I'll switch to the tool demo.
[04:53] [screen: Console -> Tools tab]
[04:58] Maya: Here we have an "action-handler" tool configured: URL points to their staging endpoint, auth via signed HMAC key from KMS, and we set allowed_actions to ["schedule_appointment","order_lab"]. The route configuration maps model action types to tool bindings.
[05:20] Marco: Can the model invent arbitrary endpoints?
[05:23] Samir: No — the runtime only allows configured tools. There's a white-list and the schema must conform to the tool's input schema. If the model tries to return an unregistered action we reject and flag.
[05:36] Priya: In production we'd need audit logs and an ability to rollback.
[05:40] Avery: Console shows per-request traces with token costs, matched schema, and decision logs. In Dedicated/Private we persist logs to your S3 or your SIEM, and you can route audit events to your Splunk/Elastic. Rollback? For tool side effects we recommend staging + approval flow: model suggests action -> human approves in UI -> Redwood will call tool. Or you can configure auto-approve for non-critical actions.
[06:10] Lena: Data residency and encryption?
[06:13] Samir: Hosted: encrypted at rest with customer-specific KMS keys, TLS in flight. For Private we integrate with your KMS/HSM. We also support VPC-only egress. We'll send you a compliance package.
[06:28] [07:00] Demo continues: Samir runs a live API call with their sample note. The model returns a JSON object with a minor transcription glitch: 'diagnosis_code':'I10  ' (extra space) and 'severity':'mildish' (non-enum).
[07:25] Samir: Here the runtime canonicalizer maps 'mildish' -> 'mild' via enum_synonyms and trims codes. You'll see the trace showing 'mapped value: mild (from mildish)'.
[07:40] Marco: What if mapping is wrong? Need human-in-the-loop.
[07:44] Samir: You can set "auto_patch":false and then the status comes back 'validation_warning' and we push to a human review queue. We also send confidence scores per field.
[07:58] Priya: Can we run end-to-end tests?
[08:02] Samir: Yes. Optimize has an evaluation harness where you can upload a prompt set and expected JSON outputs and run regression alerts. We'll show that in a follow-up recording.
[08:18] Maya: Now tool call demo: model suggests order_lab action with payload {patient_id, lab_code, urgency}. Because this action is registered the runtime signs the payload and posts to the staging tool endpoint. In our demo we have auto-approve off, so the action is queued and appears in the operator UI for approval.
[08:45] Lena: Do you support SAML/SSO for operator UI?
[08:48] Avery: Yes, SSO + SCIM provisioning + RBAC for roles.
[08:54] Marco: Anything around PII redaction?
[08:56] Samir: We have built-in PII detectors and redaction hooks; you can mask fields before tool calls or strip them from logs. In Private you can opt-out of any logging.
[09:12] [minor crosstalk; background noise]
[09:20] Priya: On costs: can you give a ballpark for a 10k-monthly report generation workload?
[09:26] Samir: Roughly — hosted with structured model and light canonicalization might be around $X per 1k reports (we'll calculate precisely). The big levers are sequence length, frequency of re-asks, and whether you stream or batch. We suggested Optimize heuristics: batching for high-throughput nightly jobs, strict_mode with patching for real-time low-latency.
[09:50] Marco: For the pilot we want two routes: realtime summarization (low-latency, human approval on actions) and nightly batch normalization (throughput-optimized).
[09:59] Avery: Perfect. We'll propose an architecture and cost estimate.
[10:05] [wrap-up]
[10:07] Avery: Recap: we'll send the recording and schema examples, Samir will prepare a perf plan, Marco will share prompt set, and we'll aim to kick off pilot week of 2025-12-10. Any blockers?
[10:22] Lena: Need SOC2 docs and clear SLA options.
[10:25] Avery: We'll include SOC2 snapshot and Dedicated/Private pricing tiers.
[10:30] Maya: I'll drop the Console recording and the two example schemas into email.
[10:35] Marco: Thanks, that was helpful.
[10:38] [meeting ends]

Notes on transcript quality: automated transcript picked up some terms incorrectly — e.g., "KV cache" as "KV cash", "VPC" sometimes as "V-P-C". We preserved a few filler words and overlaps to keep it realistic.

References shared: Console recording link (link: https://redwood.ai/console-recordings/ff-20251203-nova), JSON schema examples (link: https://redwood.ai/examples/nova-json-schemas), Pilot perf plan template (link: https://redwood.ai/templates/pilot-perf).
